source_refs.note: Topic 5.8, printed pages 105-106, as printed: the liquid-vapour equilibrium as an equation, Figure 5.8 (original drawing) and Quick Check 5.6. The print's 'Fig (5.11)' is marked.

blocks.text: The molecules of a liquid which leave the open surface are mixed up with air above the liquid. If the vessel is open these molecules go on leaving the surface of liquid. But if we close the system the molecules of liquid start gathering above the surface. These molecules collide with the walls of the container, and also with the surface of the liquid as well. There are chances that these molecules are recaptured by the surface of liquid. This process is called condensation. The two processes, i.e., evaporation and condensation continue till a stage reaches when the rate of evaporation becomes equal to the rate of condensation Fig (5.11).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed reference “Fig (5.11)” should read Figure 5.8, which shows evaporation and condensation reaching equilibrium.
The pressure exerted by the liquid vapour in equilibrium with its liquid at a given temperature is called vapour pressure.

The magnitude of vapour pressure does not depend upon the amount of liquid in the container or the volume of container. It does not depend on surface area of a liquid. The larger surface area presents a larger target for returning the molecules, so the rate of condensation also increases.

blocks.alt: Three closed boxes side by side, each with dotted liquid at the bottom and arrows at the liquid surface. (a) Vacuum above the liquid: six arrows point up, molecules only leave. (b) Vapour: four arrows up and two down, some molecules return. (c) Vapour: arrows alternate up and down, three each, so evaporation and condensation go on at the same rate.
blocks.caption: Figure 5.8: Attainment of equilibrium when the evaporation of liquid is carried out in an evacuated closed vessel. (a) Initial state, with evacuated space above the liquid, (b) intermediate state, and (c) equilibrium state, when the rate of evaporation is equal to the rate of condensation.

blocks.prompt:
a) Which of the liquids in each of the following pairs has a higher vapour pressure?
i) Alcohol, glycerine
ii) Petrol, kerosene,
iii) Mercury, water?
blocks.explanation: A liquid with weaker intermolecular forces evaporates more easily and has a higher vapour pressure: (i) alcohol (one O−H group, against three in glycerine), (ii) petrol (smaller molecules, weaker London forces), (iii) water (mercury atoms are held by strong metallic bonding).

blocks.prompt: b) Which one in each of the following pairs is more viscous: Glycerine, kerosene?
blocks.explanation: Glycerine, because its three O−H groups form many hydrogen bonds; kerosene has only London forces.

blocks.prompt: c) Separate portions of acetone and water at the same temperature are poured on your hands. The acetone feels colder. Account for this in terms of attractive forces.
blocks.explanation: The forces between acetone molecules are weaker than those in water (hydrogen bonds), so acetone evaporates much faster and takes heat away from the skin faster.

blocks.prompt: d) Why evaporation gets faster at higher temperatures?
blocks.explanation: At a higher temperature more molecules have enough kinetic energy to overcome the attractive forces at the surface and escape, so more molecules leave every second.
